blocks.text: Equal keys under the table’s equality relation must have equal hashes. The converse is not required: unequal keys may collide. If a custom equality policy treats two identifiers as equivalent while the hash policy sends them to different candidate regions, a lookup can miss an existing equivalent entry. Design equality and hashing as one coherent policy, not as unrelated utility functions.

blocks.text: Stored keys must retain the properties used to organize them. The hash table’s own links may remain intact while its lookup invariant has been broken by an external mutation. Owned immutable keys or a disciplined lifetime and mutation contract prevent that class of defect.

topics.summary: Good distribution spreads expected keys so candidate sets and probe sequences remain short. Load factor compares stored entries with available buckets or slots, but identical load factors can behave differently under clustering or adversarial keys.

blocks.text: Average constant-time claims require assumptions about distribution and operation costs. Worst-case lookup can be linear when many keys collide or a probing table becomes congested. Measure probe lengths or bucket lengths in addition to wall time when investigating performance. A hash table that happens to pass a small random test is not automatically resistant to malicious collision patterns.

blocks.text: Load factor summarizes occupancy, but it does not describe the complete distribution. Two tables with eight entries and sixteen slots can have very different lookup behavior if one spreads entries evenly and the other forms a long cluster. Measure maximum and typical bucket lengths or probe counts when diagnosing a table rather than reporting only total size.

blocks.text: For chaining, a simple expected-cost argument assumes keys distribute reasonably across m buckets. With n entries, the average bucket population is n/m. That ratio helps explain why growth can maintain short candidate scans. It does not prove that an individual bucket is short or that an externally chosen workload satisfies the assumption.

blocks.text: For linear probing, occupied runs matter because each collision pushes a key into a later slot, potentially joining neighboring clusters. Deleted slots marked as tombstones also affect future searches even though they do not count as live entries. A table can have low live occupancy but long probe paths after many deletions. Tracking live count and used-or-deleted count separately can inform a rebuild policy.

blocks.text: The worked tables deliberately do not rehash. Their tests use a bounded key domain and enough open-addressed slots to accommodate that domain. blocks.text: When a table is slow, ask whether the cause is collision distribution, excessive load, expensive key comparison, allocation, or cache behavior. blocks.text: Insertion remembers the first reusable slot but continues far enough to find an already existing key. Stopping immediately at the first tombstone can create a duplicate key instead of updating the later entry. Every scan is bounded by the slot count, so a full or all-tombstone table terminates. A full insertion with no existing key and no reusable slot returns false rather than looping indefinitely.

reading.title: Guided lab — Force collisions and test the model
paragraphs: Build an exercise table with a configurable hash policy and supply a constant hash for tests. This is not a performance recommendation. It is a deliberate way to force every key through the same collision path regardless of standard-library implementation details.

Enumerate short operation histories over three keys and two values using insert/update, get, and erase. Compare with a simple vector of unique key/value pairs maintained by linear search. The slow reference is valuable because its mechanism differs from the hash implementation. Use capacities one through four so full and tombstone states occur frequently.

Instrument probes without changing lookup semantics. Report the count for successful lookup, unsuccessful lookup, update, and rejected insertion. Run a sequence that fills the table, deletes most entries, and performs missing lookups. Explain why low live size need not imply short searches when many tombstones remain.

Design a rehash transaction. Allocate a new table, reinsert only live entries, verify the same mapping, and publish the new storage after success. State whether failure preserves the original table. Include peak temporary storage in the design. Do not copy slot indices or assume that a tombstone is a live key.
